title: "How do I recover them?"

[District 4]{.district}

## There is no short answer

::: block
From the previous districts you know three things: what genome your virus
carries, who it infects, and what kind of sample it is hiding in.

[Those three decide how you recover it.]{.claim}

That is what we will explore in this district.
:::

::: research
**What this district recommends comes from our own experience.** Every fork has
alternatives, and there may be techniques not described here that suit your
study better. Use it as a starting point, not a boundary: read further, and ask
people who have done it. What it leaves out is left out on purpose: possible,
but not standard practice.
:::

::: {.question .wide}
- Am I looking for DNA, RNA, or both?
- Who is it infecting?
- What kind of sample do I have?
:::

## Am I looking for DNA, RNA, or both?

::: block
Have you ever wondered why the flu vaccine is given every year, while one shot
of the smallpox vaccine was enough for life? It comes down to how each virus
copies itself. Most RNA viruses copy without checking their work: mistakes slip
through, and the virus drifts so fast that within a year your immune system no
longer recognises it. Most DNA viruses proofread as they go, and stay almost the
same for decades.

That speed is an advantage for the virus. Mutating fast is what lets it escape a
body that already knows it. For you it is a different problem: RNA is a fragile
molecule and it falls apart easily, so catching an RNA virus calls for careful
handling, and it has to be turned into DNA before it can be sequenced at all.
:::

::: block
That is because sequencers read double-stranded DNA. Whatever your genome is,
it has to get there first, and how far it has to travel depends on what it
started as.

- [1]{.n} [**RNA** — reverse transcription, RNA to cDNA.]{.t}
- [2]{.n} [**Single-stranded** — second-strand synthesis.]{.t}
- [3]{.n} [**Double-stranded DNA** — already there.]{.t}

Then library prep, which is what makes any of it readable: short known
sequences called **adapters** go on both ends of every fragment, so the machine
has somewhere to grab on and start. Then into the run.

One thing runs through all that copying. A polymerase cannot begin from nothing.
It needs a short piece already paired to the template, a **primer**, to build out
from, so every step above begins with a choice of primer, and that choice
decides what gets copied and what is missed.

![Reverse transcription, step by step. The template is RNA; what reaches the library is double-stranded DNA.](../assets/img/reverse_transcription_compact_six_step_strip.svg){#fig-rt fig-alt="Six panels showing reverse transcription: viral RNA template, priming with random hexamers, extension by RT enzyme, RNA cleared by RNase H, second strand by DNA polymerase, and the finished double-stranded product."}
:::

::: methodology
**Do not let the primer choose for you.** The usual way to prime RNA is
oligo-dT, which anneals to the run of A's that caps most host messenger RNA.
Plenty of viral genomes carry no such tail, so an oligo-dT prep quietly hands
back the host and little else. Random hexamers are short primers of every
possible sequence: they start anywhere, and they do not care what they are
starting on.
:::

::: block
Random priming has a cost that oligo-dT does not: it copies whatever is in the
tube. Reagent background, carry-over from the tube beside it — to a random
primer, all of it is template.
:::

::: methodology
**Two water controls, not one.** Run a blank as the first sample of the batch
and another as the last. The first tells you whether a reagent arrived
contaminated; the last tells you whether signal moved from tube to tube while
you worked. One blank cannot tell those apart, and they have different fixes —
a new aliquot in one case, a change in how you handle the bench in the other.
:::

## Who is it infecting?

::: block
Answer this one before you touch a protocol, because it decides whether the main
enrichment step in virome work applies to you at all. A virus infecting a human
cell is usually out in the open as a free particle. A phage may be out there
too, or it may be sitting inside the chromosome of the bacterium it infected, in
which case it is not a particle at all.

Why that matters: remember the noise problem from District 3, where the virus is
a sliver under everything else. There is a way to lift that fraction before
sequencing, **VLP enrichment**, for virus-like particles.

The principle is a series of gates, each removing things by a physical property.
Filter out cells and debris by size; digest free nucleic acid with nucleases.
What survives is encapsidated: a genome inside a protein shell is protected from
the enzymes, and everything naked is not.

![One VLP protocol, end to end. Volumes, speeds and timings are this laboratory's; the sequence of gates is general.](../assets/img/lab_vlp_enrichment_magnapure_seven_step_strip.svg){#fig-vlp fig-alt="Seven panels of a VLP enrichment protocol: chip and weigh frozen stool, homogenise in SM buffer, clarify by centrifugation, filter at 0.45 micrometres, digest with lysozyme and DNase, stop with EDTA, and extract on a MagNA Pure."}
:::

::: fivi
![](../assets/img/fivi-annoyed.png){fig-alt="Fivi, annoyed."}

**Enrichment does not purify me — it selects for me.** Every gate is a physical
property, not a test for "virus". Some of what passes is not viral, and some of
what I am is thrown out with the rest. A VLP prep is a bet on the shape you are
chasing.
:::

::: methodology
**An integrated target does not survive it.** A provirus, a prophage or an ERV
is not a free particle: it sits inside a host genome, so the filter removes it
with the cell and the nuclease digests what is left. If you are looking for
integrated viruses, skip VLP and sequence total nucleic acid.
:::

::: research
There is no standard VLP protocol. Filter pore size, nuclease cocktail, gradient
step and extraction chemistry all differ between laboratories, and each choice
shifts which particles survive. Two published "viromes" from the same body site
may not be comparable if the preps differ — read the methods before you compare
composition across studies.
:::

## When does enrichment cost more than it gains?

::: block
Enrichment is not free, and it is not always right. It removes things — and
some of what it removes is what you came for.
:::

## Is my sample rich in bacteria?

::: block
You have just seen what enrichment costs. The last question is whether your
sample can pay it, and that comes down to how much is living in it. A gram of
stool and a millilitre of plasma are not the same starting point: one is dense
with material, the other is mostly you.

Sampling sites sort into four kinds, and the sort is what decides whether VLP
applies at all.

- [**Mucosal**]{.t} [gut, mouth, throat, vagina. Colonised and dense, with the bacteria and the phages that live in them. **This is where VLP belongs.**]{.t}
- [**Transitional**]{.t} [milk, urine, skin. Secretions, excretions and outer surfaces: some community, much less of it.]{.t}
- [**Sterile fluids**]{.t} [blood, CSF, lung. A community is there to find, but no resident bacteria, so no prophages either, and very little material to start from.]{.t}
- [**Solid tissue**]{.t} [a biopsy. There is nothing to fractionate: no free particles to filter for.]{.t}

Only the first of those four is a candidate for enrichment.
:::

::: methodology
**Very low biomass does not survive it either.** Blood, CSF and other sparse
sites give you little material to begin with, and every gate loses some. Do not
filter; sample with great care instead, and carry heavy controls and replicates.
:::

::: block
Look back at how many forks this district asked you to take: the genome you are
chasing, who it infects and whether it is a particle at all, the sample you have
to work with, and whether to enrich it. None of them is decided on its own, and
no chapter can decide them for your sample.

So we built something that takes the details of your experiment and works them
through for you.
:::

::: insight
One fork is left, and it is the one that matters least. Short reads are the
default and, for most viromes, the right answer: they cost less, they go deeper
for the same money, and every tool in the next district was built for them. Long
reads earn their cost only when the question is structural, like where a prophage
sits in its host chromosome or whether two contigs belong to one genome.
:::

::: fivi
![](../assets/img/fivi-thinking.png){fig-alt="Fivi, thinking."}

**That is the bench done.** Everything so far decided what physically reaches the
sequencer. What comes back is a pile of reads, and none of it is sorted yet —
that is the [next district](bioinformatics.qmd).
:::
